newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Rains delay non-stop crushing of Brazil NNE sugar.
newsitem.headline: Rains delay non-stop crushing of Brazil NNE sugar.

text.p: Factories in Brazil's north/northeast sugar producing region will only really begin non-stop crushing by the end of this week after rain has led to a two-week delay, an independent analyst said.
"There has been a delay in the start of uninterrupted crushing due to a prolonged rainy period," said Aloisio Sotero, of Recife-based consultants DataNet-Agricommodities.
"This would normally have taken place by September 15 but now will only begin this week," he added.
Carlos Novaes, spokesman at the regional cooperative for Alagoas State Sugar and Alcohol producers, said that of the 11 mills in the cooperative, only five were this week beginning to work non-stop.
"The forecast had been for September 15 but the rains have caused delays in the harvest. But all the factories should be working full-time from next week," Novaes said.

Alagoas is the largest producing state in the region which Sotero estimates in total should produce 48.5 million tonnes of sugar cane, up from last year's 47.1 million tonnes but well below other industry forecasts of a 10 percent increase.

Earlier this week the Industry and Commerce Ministry circulated a report containing a forecast of a 50 million tonne harvest in the area, up from the 48 million tonnes included in the June official crop plan.

Sugar production should reach 3.35 million tonnes of which 1.75 million tonnes will be exported, according to Sotero, slightly higher than the 3.21 million and 1.52 million tonnes respectively contained in the crop plan.
"My sugar cane estimate allows for a three percent increase," Sotero said.

"But if you ring sugar producing unions, they will say that there will be a 10 percent rise. It's true the climate has been good but many mills have stopped operating because of high interest rates," Sotero said.

Weather will continue to be a key factor throughout the crushing season as growers are unable to look after the crop as well as usual due to financial constraints, making it more vulnerable to climatic changes, he added.
So far there have only been a few exports of new crop sugar from the north/northeast.
While these are expected to pick up in the next month, there should be no marked impact from the recent lifting of the so-called ICMS state tax on raw and semi-manufactured goods, Sotero said.
"I have seen many reports saying that the scrapping of the ICMS tax will improve sugar exports this year but it will have a very limited impact for sugar," he said.

"The lifting of the tax affects demerara sugar and while the north/northeast is traditionally a big exporter of this sugar, there are already petitions in the law courts which have meant sugar has been exported tax-free since last year," Sotero said.
